Accounts

The Complete Guide to CRA Accounts on a Dormant Corporation

A business number carries separate accounts, and each one keeps its own obligations until it is closed. What a dormant corporation still owes, and how to end it. Nil T2 filing is $300.00 plus HST per tax year.

Written and reviewed by Sharad Gondaliya, CPA (Ontario), CPA Ontario Membership 61040184.

Start Nil T2 Filing NOWSequence the closures

Last reviewed: October 29, 2026  ·  All nil T2 filing guides

On this page

  1. A Business Number Is Not One Account
  2. The Obligation Follows the Account, Not the Activity
  3. The GST/HST Account: Nil Returns Until It Is Closed
  4. The Payroll Account: Remittances and an Annual T4
  5. Form RC145 Closes Both of Them
  6. Why These Two Accounts Reach the Directors
  7. The Corporate Income Tax Account Is Different
  8. The Order to Deal With Them In
  9. What Has to Be Closed Before a Dissolution
  10. What Sits Outside the Fee, Said Plainly
  11. The Four Mistakes Worth Avoiding
  12. What the Fee Covers

Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation is a registered EFILE electronic filer. Returns are prepared and transmitted in Canada. Credentials are never shared and never used offshore.

A Business Number Is Not One Account

A corporation has one business number, and that number carries separate program accounts. The corporate income tax account is the one everybody knows about, because it is the one the T2 is filed against. It is rarely the one that causes trouble.

A corporation that ever had staff has a payroll account. One that ever registered for GST/HST has a GST/HST account. Each was opened for a reason, and each stays open until somebody closes it, whatever happened to the reason.

AccountOpened becauseWhat it expectsHow it ends
Corporate income taxThe corporation existsA T2 return for every tax yearIt ends with the corporation
PayrollSomeone was going to be paidRemittances through the year and an annual T4 information returnForm RC145
GST/HSTThe corporation registeredA GST/HST return for every reporting periodForm RC145

The business number status checker works through which of them a given corporation is likely to have open.

The Obligation Follows the Account, Not the Activity

This is the sentence that explains almost every unpleasant surprise a dormant corporation gets. The Canada Revenue Agency expects a return on an open account because the account is open. It does not wait to see whether anything happened first.

So a corporation that stopped trading four years ago, paid nobody and sold nothing, still has returns falling due on every account nobody closed. Each one is a separate filing with its own deadline, and none of them is the T2.

Being dormant is not a status you register. There is no form that tells the Agency a corporation has gone quiet and no notification that pauses an account. Nothing happens until an account is closed, and until then the dates keep arriving.

The guide to dormant and inactive corporations covers what being dormant does and does not change.

The GST/HST Account: Nil Returns Until It Is Closed

An open GST/HST account expects a return for every reporting period, and a period with no sales and no tax collected is reported as a nil return rather than skipped. The return is what the account expects; having nothing to report changes the figures on it, not whether it is filed.

That catches people out twice. Once because they assume no activity means no return, and again because the reporting period is often quarterly or monthly, so a single forgotten account generates four or twelve outstanding returns a year rather than one.

The GST/HST nil filing checker tests whether an account is in that position, and the GST/HST account closure checker covers ending it.

The Payroll Account: Remittances and an Annual T4

An open payroll account expects two separate things, which is why it is the account most often underestimated. Through the year it expects remittances, including nil ones where nobody was paid. After the calendar year it expects a T4 information return.

The T4 deadline is the one that surprises accountants as well as owners, because it does not derive from the fiscal year-end at all. It reports a calendar year and is due at the end of the following February, whatever year-end the corporation uses.

What the payroll account expectsMeasured fromDue
Remittances, including nil onesEach remittance periodFor as long as the account is open
The T4 information returnThe calendar yearThe end of the following February

So a corporation with a June 30 year-end has a T2 date in December and a T4 date at the end of February, four months apart, neither derived from the other. The T4 nil filing requirement checker gives the date, and the payroll nil remittance checker covers the remittances.

Nil T2 Filing, $300.00 plus HST per tax year

One price for every year and every province. CPA reviewed and transmitted electronically.

Start Nil T2 Filing NOW

Form RC145 Closes Both of Them

One form closes a payroll account and the same form closes a GST/HST account. It is the only thing that ends the obligations on either: not inactivity, not telling an accountant, not letting the returns lapse.

Until the account is closed, nil returns and nil remittances remain due on it, and they accumulate exactly as an unfiled T2 does. A closure is also not retroactive in the way people hope. Closing an account today does not file the returns that fell due on it while it was open, and it does not clear what was owed on it.

This is why the order matters, and the order is the outstanding returns first, then the closure. A closure stacked on top of unfiled periods leaves the unfiled periods exactly where they were.

Why These Two Accounts Reach the Directors

The corporate income tax account is the corporation’s own liability. The other two are not, and that distinction is the practical reason an unused payroll or GST/HST account is worth closing rather than ignoring.

Payroll source deductions are money withheld from someone’s pay. Net GST/HST is money collected from customers. Neither was ever the corporation’s to keep, and amounts of that kind can be assessed against a corporation’s directors personally. Corporate income tax, on its own, cannot.

AmountWhose money it wasCan be assessed against a director
Payroll source deductionsWithheld from someone’s payYes
Net GST/HSTCollected from customersYes
Corporate income taxThe corporation’s own liabilityNo, not on its own

A dormant corporation rarely owes corporate income tax, because a nil year assesses at $0.00. What it may have is an open account generating exactly the amounts that do reach a director. The director liability exposure checker sorts which is which.

The Corporate Income Tax Account Is Different

There is no form that closes it while the corporation exists, and nothing to close: the account is the corporation’s relationship with the Agency for income tax, and it ends when the corporation does.

So the T2 is not something that can be switched off for a quiet year. Every tax year gets a return until the corporation is dissolved, and a year with no activity gets one reporting $0.00 rather than no return at all.

A true nil return carries no percentage late-filing penalty, because that penalty is a percentage of tax owing and the corporation owes $0.00. The unfiled year still stays open forever, invites a demand to file and an arbitrary assessment, blocks a clearance certificate and dissolution, and costs a non-resident-owned corporation $25.00 per day up to $2,500.00.

The complete guide to the nil T2 return is the pillar for that side of it.

The Order to Deal With Them In

The sequence is not arbitrary, because each step rests on the one before it. Returns first, because a closure does not file anything. Closures next, because they stop the dates recurring. Anything to do with dissolution last, because it rests on a complete filing record.

OrderStepWhy it sits here
1File every outstanding T2 return, oldest firstEach year opens from the closing balances of the one before it
2File the outstanding GST/HST and payroll returnsA closure does not file what fell due while the account was open
3Close the payroll account with Form RC145Ends the remittances and the annual T4
4Close the GST/HST account with Form RC145Ends the reporting periods
5The final T2, clearance and the registry filingOnly where the corporation is being wound up

The CRA account closure sequencer produces this list for a particular corporation, naming which steps apply and which sit outside the fee.

What Has to Be Closed Before a Dissolution

A corporation cannot be cleanly wound up with accounts still open and returns still outstanding. The clearance certificate is the step that makes this concrete: the request rests on a complete filing record, so an outstanding GST/HST or payroll period blocks it as surely as an unfiled T2.

Dissolving anyway does not solve it. A corporation dissolved with unfiled years leaves those years open behind it, and the registry dissolution settles nothing on the tax side.

The guide to winding up an inactive corporation sets out the whole sequence, and the dissolution readiness checker tests whether a corporation is ready for the last step.

What Sits Outside the Fee, Said Plainly

The fee of $300.00 plus HST per tax year covers one nil T2 return for one corporation for one tax year. It is worth being direct about what that does not include, because the accounts on this page are the commonest place the boundary gets found the hard way.

ItemCovered by the fee
A nil T2 return for a tax yearYes
A GST/HST return, nil or otherwiseNo
A payroll remittance, nil or otherwiseNo
The T4 information returnNo
Closing an account with Form RC145No
The registry annual returnNo
A clearance certificate requestNo

Where any of those are needed, they are handled by Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation at gondaliyacpa.ca rather than priced here. The full boundary is on the nil T2 filing cost page.

The Four Mistakes Worth Avoiding

Each of these is common enough to be worth naming, and each one costs more to undo than to avoid.

The mistakeWhat it actually does
Assuming no activity means no returnThe obligation follows the open account, so the returns fall due anyway and accumulate
Closing an account to deal with the outstanding returnsA closure files nothing. The outstanding periods stay outstanding
Reading the T4 deadline off the fiscal year-endThe T4 reports a calendar year and is due at the end of the following February, which can be months away from the T2 date
Dissolving with accounts still openThe tax years stay open behind the dissolution, and a clearance certificate is blocked until they are filed

The thread running through all four is the same: an account is a standing obligation, and only a closure ends it. The guide to the corporate compliance calendar sets out the dates each open account generates.

Schedule 50For every shareholder at 10% or more

Frequently Asked Questions

Does a dormant corporation still have to file GST/HST returns?

While the account is open, yes. A period with no sales is reported as a nil return rather than skipped, because the obligation follows the open account rather than the activity.

Do I have to make payroll remittances if nobody was paid?

While the payroll account is open the Agency expects the remittances, including nil ones, and a T4 information return after each calendar year. Form RC145 closes the account and ends both.

How do I close a GST/HST or payroll account?

With Form RC145, which closes either one. Closing it does not file the returns that fell due while it was open, so the outstanding returns come first.

Which of these can be assessed against me personally?

Payroll source deductions and net GST/HST can be assessed against directors personally, because neither was ever the corporation’s money. Corporate income tax, on its own, cannot.

Is any of this covered by the nil T2 fee?

The nil T2 return is. The GST/HST returns, the payroll remittances, the T4 return and the account closures all sit outside the fee of $300.00 plus HST per tax year.

Can I dissolve the corporation instead of dealing with these?

Not cleanly. A clearance certificate request rests on a complete filing record, so an outstanding period blocks it, and dissolving anyway leaves the tax years open behind the corporation.

content:
Year-End

The Complete Guide to Choosing and Changing a Fiscal Year-End

A corporation picks its own year-end, the first return fixes it, and changing it needs written approval. How to choose it and what a change costs. Nil T2 filing is $300.00 plus HST per tax year.

Written and reviewed by Sharad Gondaliya, CPA (Ontario), CPA Ontario Membership 61040184.

Start Nil T2 Filing NOWSee every date available

Last reviewed: October 29, 2026  ·  All nil T2 filing guides

On this page

  1. Nothing Assigns You a Year-End
  2. The First Tax Year Cannot Exceed 53 Weeks
  3. Everything Else Is Measured From It
  4. A Short First Year Is a Return for Almost Nothing
  5. A Short Year Does Not Get an Early Deadline
  6. Changing It Needs Written Approval
  7. A Wrong Year-End Gets the Transmission Rejected
  8. A Change Cannot Reach More Than 53 Weeks Out
  9. Why the Year-End Matters Most on a Catch-Up
  10. None of This Changes for a Nil Year
  11. How to Decide, in Practice
  12. What the Fee Covers

Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation is a registered EFILE electronic filer. Returns are prepared and transmitted in Canada. Credentials are never shared and never used offshore.

Nothing Assigns You a Year-End

A corporation picks its own fiscal year-end. There is no default, nothing is allocated at incorporation, and December 31 is a convention rather than a rule. The articles of incorporation do not set it either.

What sets it is the first T2 return filed. From then on the date is on the record, it recurs annually, and every other date in the corporation’s tax life is measured from it. That makes this the one decision that is free to make now and awkward to revisit.

The first T2 year-end options generator lists every date available from a given incorporation date, with the filing deadline each one produces.

The First Tax Year Cannot Exceed 53 Weeks

This is the one hard limit on the choice. A first tax year runs from the date of incorporation to the chosen year-end and may not exceed 53 weeks, which is 371 days counting the day of incorporation.

A year-end beyond that point is not available at all. Where someone wants one anyway, the consequence is not a longer first year: it is a first year ending earlier, then a full year, and two returns due within months of each other.

Counting it by eye from two dates in different years is where the mistakes come from, because 371 days does not line up with any month boundary. The 53-week first tax year checker tests one proposed date and the fiscal period length calculator measures a period you already have.

Everything Else Is Measured From It

Picking the year-end picks the rest of the calendar, which is the real reason it deserves a decision rather than a default. Two of these dates follow from it directly and one deliberately does not.

ObligationMeasured from the year-endWhen
The T2 returnYesSix months after it
A balance of taxYesTwo months after it, or three for a qualifying CCPC
The T4 information returnNoThe end of February following the calendar year
The registry annual returnNoMeasured from the incorporation anniversary

A month-end year-end makes the six-month rule land on a month-end too, which is the practical argument for choosing one. A year-end on the 9th puts the filing deadline on an awkward mid-month date every year after. The corporate deadline calendar generator shows the whole calendar one year-end produces.

A Short First Year Is a Return for Almost Nothing

Choose the earliest month-end after incorporating and the first tax year might be three weeks long. It is still a tax year, it still gets a return, and that return is $300.00 plus HST per tax year like any other. There is no part-year rate.

So an early first year-end means paying for a return covering almost nothing, and then a second return for the first full year. A year-end closer to twelve months out produces one return instead of two over the same stretch of time.

Short years also arise for reasons nobody chooses: an approved change of year-end, an amalgamation, and a final period ending at dissolution. The short tax year deadline calculator covers the deadline on any of them, and the guide to first-year T2 filing covers the first return itself.

Nil T2 Filing, $300.00 plus HST per tax year

One price for every year and every province. CPA reviewed and transmitted electronically.

Start Nil T2 Filing NOW

A Short Year Does Not Get an Early Deadline

Worth stating on its own because the intuition runs the other way. The six-month rule is measured from the day the period ends, whatever the period’s length. A three-month stub period has six months after it to file, which is twice the period itself.

What a short period does bring forward is the next year-end, and with it the next return. That is how two filing deadlines end up weeks apart, and how the earlier one gets missed: two dates close together read as one obligation. The two T2 returns in one year checker shows both dates and the gap between them.

Changing It Needs Written Approval

A fiscal year-end is fixed by the first return filed, and changing it needs the written approval of the Canada Revenue Agency. The request is made before the change rather than demonstrated by filing.

That sequence is the part most often got wrong, and the next section is about what happens when it is.

An approved change closes a period on the new date. That period is a tax year in its own right with its own return and its own deadline, so the cost of a change is an extra return that would not otherwise exist. The year-end change impact calculator shows the period a given change creates, its length and both filing dates.

A Wrong Year-End Gets the Transmission Rejected

Filing a return carrying a year-end that does not match the record is not read as a change of year-end. It is rejected against the date on record.

The consequence is worse than it first sounds, because a rejection is not a late filing. A refused transmission is not a filed return at all, so the year stays outstanding and the person who sent it believes it is done.

On a catch-up this compounds. Several years sent in one sitting against the wrong year-end are several years still outstanding, and the error is only found when a demand to file arrives or a clearance request is refused.

Which is why the year-end on record is confirmed before anything is transmitted rather than assumed from the incorporation papers. The corporate fiscal year end calculator works from the date on record.

A Change Cannot Reach More Than 53 Weeks Out

The same 53-week limit that bounds a first tax year bounds the period a change creates. Where the gap between the current year-end and the proposed one is longer than 371 days, that gap is not a single tax year and cannot be reported as one.

Reaching a year-end that far out needs an intervening year-end first, which means two returns rather than one. It is the same arithmetic as the first-year limit, applied at a different moment.

Length of the period a change createsWhat it is
Under twelve monthsA short tax year, with its own return
Twelve monthsA full tax year
Up to 371 daysStill one tax year
More than 371 daysNot one tax year; an intervening year-end is needed

Why the Year-End Matters Most on a Catch-Up

A corporation with one year to file has one date to get right. A corporation with six has the same date six times, and every one of those returns is rejected if the date is wrong.

The years are also prepared oldest first, because each one opens from the closing balances of the one before it. A wrong year-end does not stop at six rejections; it produces a sequence that cannot be reconciled.

The guide to catching up on unfiled corporate tax returns covers the sequence, and the catch-up filing schedule generator produces the dated schedule once the year-end is known.

None of This Changes for a Nil Year

A corporation that has never traded still has a year-end, still has it fixed by its first return, and still needs written approval to change it. Being nil affects the figures on the return and nothing about the calendar.

A holding corporation with investment income, a rental corporation and a corporation that paid or received a dividend are not nil. Those are handled by Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation at gondaliyacpa.ca at $350.00 plus HST per year.

So the year-end decision is made at incorporation whether or not anything is happening yet, and a corporation registered and left dormant has already made it by the time its first return goes in.

How to Decide, in Practice

There is no answer that fits every corporation, and anyone offering one does not know the facts. What can be said is which considerations actually bear on it.

ConsiderationWhat it argues for
Keeping the calendar simpleA month-end, so the six-month rule lands on a month-end too
Avoiding a return for a few weeks of nothingA first year-end closer to twelve months out
Matching the year to a natural business cycleA year-end after the busy season rather than inside it
Never needing to change itThinking about the next few years now, since a change costs an extra return and needs written approval

Where the corporation is dormant and may be wound up rather than traded, the last row matters most: a year-end chosen now is the one the final return will be measured from. The guide to the final T2 and dissolution covers that end of it.

What the Fee Covers

IncludedDetail
The T2 returnIncluding the T2 Short where the corporation qualifies
GIFI Schedules 100, 125 and 141Where they are required
Schedule 24On a first return
Schedule 50For every shareholder at 10% or more
Schedule 8 and loss continuityRecorded
Form T183CORP packageWith single-use secure e-signing
CPA reviewBefore transmission
Electronic transmissionBy a registered EFILE electronic filer
One corrected transmissionIf the Agency rejects the first one
CRA confirmationEmailed within 3 business days

See the full nil T2 filing cost.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who decides my corporation’s fiscal year-end?

The corporation does. There is no default and nothing is assigned at incorporation. The first T2 return filed is what fixes the date on the record.

How long can my first tax year be?

Up to 53 weeks, which is 371 days counting the day of incorporation. A year-end beyond that is not available, so the first year has to end earlier.

Can I change my fiscal year-end later?

With the written approval of the Canada Revenue Agency. The request is made before the change, and filing a return carrying a different date does not change the date on record.

What happens if I file against the wrong year-end?

The transmission is rejected against the year-end on record. A refused transmission is not a filed return, so the year stays outstanding.

Does changing a year-end cost an extra return?

Usually. The change closes a period on the new date, that period is a tax year in its own right, and it gets its own return at $300.00 plus HST per tax year.

Does a short tax year have an earlier deadline?

No. The six-month rule runs from the day the period ends, so a three-month period gets the same six months as a full year.

content:
Provincial

The Complete Guide to Quebec CO-17 and Alberta AT1

Quebec and Alberta each collect their own corporate tax, so each has a separate return. CO-17 and AT1 are not part of the federal T2 and are not covered by the fee. Nil T2 filing is $300.00 plus HST per tax year.

Written and reviewed by Sharad Gondaliya, CPA (Ontario), CPA Ontario Membership 61040184.

Start Nil T2 Filing NOWCheck which apply

Last reviewed: October 29, 2026  ·  All nil T2 filing guides

On this page

  1. Most Provinces Collect Through the Federal Return
  2. Separate Means Separate
  3. A Quiet Year Is Quiet on Both Returns
  4. Neither Is Covered by the Fee
  5. What Decides Whether a Province Is Involved
  6. The Registry Annual Return Is a Different Thing
  7. Alberta: AT1

  9. The Federal T2 Is Still Required
  10. Both Matter at a Wind-Up
  11. The Whole of It, in Five Lines
  12. What the Fee Covers

Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation is a registered EFILE electronic filer. Returns are prepared and transmitted in Canada. Credentials are never shared and never used offshore.

Most Provinces Collect Through the Federal Return

In most of Canada a corporation files one corporate income tax return. The province levies its own corporate tax, but it is collected through the federal T2, so the federal return settles both and there is nothing separate to send.

Quebec and Alberta are the exceptions. Each administers its own corporate income tax and each has its own return. Quebec’s is CO-17, filed with Revenu Quebec. Alberta’s is AT1.

Where the corporation operatesCorporate income tax returns
QuebecThe federal T2 and CO-17
AlbertaThe federal T2 and AT1
Everywhere elseThe federal T2 on its own

Separate Means Separate

CO-17 is a separate provincial return. AT1 is a separate provincial return. That phrasing is deliberate and it is worth taking literally: neither is a schedule attached to the T2, neither is produced as a by-product of filing federally, and filing the T2 does not file either.

Each has its own form, its own filing, and its own deadline. A corporation that files a perfect T2 and nothing else has met one of its two obligations.

The provincial return requirement checker answers which of them apply to a particular corporation, in two questions.

A Quiet Year Is Quiet on Both Returns

A corporation with no activity has nothing to report provincially either, so the provincial return for that year is nil in the same way the federal one is.

Being nil does not make it optional. The obligation follows from the corporation having a permanent establishment in the province, not from there being something to report, so a nil year is still a return to file.

This is the same logic as every other obligation on a dormant corporation, and it is the single most useful thing to understand about nil filing: the question is never whether anything happened, it is whether an obligation exists. The guide to zero-activity corporate tax returns works through that distinction.

Neither Is Covered by the Fee

The fee of $300.00 plus HST per tax year covers one nil federal T2 return for one corporation for one tax year. CO-17 is not covered by it, and neither is AT1.

Stating that plainly is better than leaving it to be discovered. A corporation with a Quebec or Alberta permanent establishment needs work this service does not price, and pretending otherwise would be worse than saying so.

Where a provincial return is needed it is handled by Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation at gondaliyacpa.ca at $350.00 plus HST per year. The nil T2 filing cost page sets out the whole boundary of what sits inside the fee.

Nil T2 Filing, $300.00 plus HST per tax year

One price for every year and every province. CPA reviewed and transmitted electronically.

Start Nil T2 Filing NOW

What Decides Whether a Province Is Involved

The test is a permanent establishment in the province, not where the corporation was incorporated and not where the director happens to live. A federally incorporated corporation operating only in Quebec files CO-17; an Ontario corporation with no Quebec presence does not.

Where that test lands for a particular corporation is a question of fact rather than something a web page can settle, and it is not a question to answer by guessing. What this page can do is say which returns exist and what each one is.

A dormant corporation is usually the straightforward case: a corporation that has never operated anywhere has no permanent establishment anywhere, and the federal T2 is the whole of its corporate income tax filing.

The Registry Annual Return Is a Different Thing

This is the commonest confusion on the subject, and it is worth separating carefully, because the two obligations share the words "annual" and "provincial" and nothing else.

A provincial tax returnA registry annual return
What it isCO-17 in Quebec, AT1 in AlbertaA filing confirming the directors and the registered office
What it reportsIncome and provincial corporate taxNo income at all
Who it goes toThe provincial tax administrationThe registry the corporation is incorporated with
What missing it doesAn outstanding returnA striking: the registry dissolves the corporation

Every corporation owes a registry annual return somewhere, including the 11 provinces and territories that have no separate tax return. The guide to provincial and federal annual returns covers that obligation, and the involuntary dissolution risk checker covers what missing it produces.

Alberta: AT1

AT1 is Alberta’s corporate income tax return, and it is a separate provincial return filed with Alberta rather than part of the federal T2.

A corporation with an Alberta permanent establishment files both. A nil year produces a nil AT1 rather than no AT1, on the same reasoning as everything else here: the obligation follows the permanent establishment rather than the activity.

AT1 is not covered by the fee of $300.00 plus HST per tax year.

Quebec: CO-17

CO-17 is Quebec’s corporate income tax return, filed with Revenu Quebec. It is a separate provincial return, not a schedule of the federal T2 and not produced by filing federally.

A corporation with a Quebec permanent establishment files both. A nil year produces a nil CO-17 rather than no CO-17.

CO-17 is not covered by the fee of $300.00 plus HST per tax year.

Quebec is also the province where the two obligations on this page are most often conflated, because the registry filing and the tax return both sit with Quebec institutions. They remain separate filings with separate consequences.

The Federal T2 Is Still Required

Worth saying because the logic occasionally runs backwards: a corporation that files CO-17 or AT1 has not thereby dealt with the federal return. The T2 is required of every resident corporation, in every province, every tax year, until the corporation is dissolved.

So a Quebec corporation files two returns and an Alberta corporation files two returns. Neither replaces the other, and a nil year means two nil returns rather than one.

A true nil return carries no percentage late-filing penalty, because that penalty is a percentage of tax owing and the corporation owes $0.00. The unfiled year still stays open forever, invites a demand to file and an arbitrary assessment, blocks a clearance certificate and dissolution, and costs a non-resident-owned corporation $25.00 per day up to $2,500.00.

Both Matter at a Wind-Up

A corporation being wound up has to be current on everything, and a provincial return is part of everything. An outstanding CO-17 or AT1 is an outstanding return in the same way an unfiled T2 is.

Where a clearance certificate is being sought, the request rests on a complete filing record. The federal side of that is what this service covers; the provincial side, where it exists, is handled at gondaliyacpa.ca.

The guide to winding up an inactive corporation sets out the order the steps have to happen in, and the clearance certificate requirement checker covers the certificate itself.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Quebec have a separate corporate tax return?

Yes. CO-17 is a separate provincial return, filed with Revenu Quebec. It is not part of the federal T2, and filing the T2 does not file it.

Does Alberta have a separate corporate tax return?

Yes. AT1 is a separate provincial return in the same way, filed with Alberta rather than as part of the federal T2.

What about the other provinces and territories?

Elsewhere the province or territory collects its corporate income tax through the federal return, so the T2 is the only corporate income tax return the corporation files.

Is a nil CO-17 or AT1 still required?

The obligation follows from having a permanent establishment in the province rather than from there being something to report, so a nil year still produces a return on each one that applies.

Are CO-17 and AT1 covered by the fee?

No. The fee of $300.00 plus HST per tax year covers one nil federal T2 return for one corporation for one tax year. Provincial returns are handled by Gondaliya CPA Professional Corporation at gondaliyacpa.ca at $350.00 plus HST per year.

Is this the same as the provincial annual return?

No, and they are easy to confuse. A registry annual return confirms the directors and the registered office and reports no income; a provincial tax return reports income and tax. Missing the registry one gets a corporation struck.
